posts.title: Welcome to Strength Speed Steve
posts.excerpt: What this site is, who the coaching is for, and why strength and speed belong in the same program.
posts.alt: Steve Rose performing a kettlebell carry
posts.body:
Welcome in — I'm Steve Rose, M.S., CSCS, Assistant Performance Coach at Princeton University. This site exists for one reason: to help athletes train with a plan instead of a pile of random workouts — and that coaching is delivered through TrainHeroic.

The name says it all — strength and speed. Most programs pick one. Lift heavy and get slow, or run sprints with nothing underneath them. Done right, the two build each other: strength gives you more force to put into the ground, and speed work teaches you to use that force fast.

Who this is for

Athletes in-season and off, beginners who want to learn the lifts properly, and anyone training on their own who wants a coach's structure without guessing. If you play a sport — or train like you do — you're in the right place.

How to use this site

  • Coaching — how strength and speed training are actually run.
  • Programs — 1-on-1, online, and team options.
  • Blog — training explained plainly, starting with Speed Training 101.

When you're ready, coaching runs through TrainHeroic. To get started, DM me on Instagram with your sport and your goal and I'll point you the right way.

— Steve

posts.title: Speed Training 101
posts.excerpt: Acceleration vs. top speed, why rest matters more than reps, and a simple session you can run this week.
posts.alt: Steve Rose performing a broad jump onto a 20-inch box
posts.body:
Speed is a skill, and like every skill it falls apart when you're exhausted. That's the first thing to understand: if your “speed work” leaves you gasping, you're training conditioning — useful, but it's not making you faster.

The two kinds of speed

Acceleration is your first steps — roughly the first 10 to 30 yards — where you're driving forward at an angle and every step pushes you ahead. Max velocity is top-end speed: upright, tall, and all about how much force you can put down in the shortest contact with the ground. They look different, they feel different, and they get trained with different distances.

The rules that make it work

  • Short reps. Most true speed reps last under 7 seconds.
  • Full rest. Walk back, wait, breathe — a rough guide is about a minute of rest for every 10 yards sprinted.
  • Fresh legs. Sprint before lifting, or on its own day. Never at the end of a hard session.
  • Stop when you slow down. If the times drop off, the speed work is done. More tired reps only teach you to run slow.

A simple first session

Warm up thoroughly — jogging, skips, and a few build-up runs. Then: 6 × 20-yard accelerations from a standing or falling start, full walk-back rest between reps. Finish there. As the weeks go on, stretch the distance out and add a few flying sprints for top-end work.

Pair that with two or three full-body lift days a week — squat, hinge, press, pull — and you have the foundation of every program on this site: strong enough to produce force, fast enough to use it.
